questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If I had known, I would have called you.
If I knew, I would have called you yesterday.
If I had knew, I would called you.
If I would have known, I called you.
questions.e: For an unreal past condition, use “if + had + past participle” and “would have + past participle”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The report was written by Amina.
The report was wrote by Amina.
The report has written by Amina yesterday.
questions.e: The passive past uses “was + past participle”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Not until the bell rang the students did leave.
Not until rang the bell did the students leave.
Not until the bell rang did the students leave.
Not until the bell did rang the students leave.
questions.e: After “Not until” at the beginning, use inversion: “did the students leave”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She suggested to go by bus.
She suggested us going by bus.
questions.e: After “suggest”, use a noun or an “-ing” form.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Despite being tired, he finished the work.
Despite he was tired, he finished the work.
Despite of being tired, he finished the work.
Despite to be tired, he finished the work.
questions.e: After “despite”, use a noun or an “-ing” form.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He denied to take the money.
He denied that taking the money.
questions.e: After “deny”, use an “-ing” form.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Had we left earlier, we would catch the bus yesterday.
Had we leave earlier, we would have caught the bus.
Had we left earlier, we would have caught the bus.
Had we would left earlier, we caught the bus.
questions.e: This inverted third conditional means “If we had left earlier…”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The more you practise, more confident you become.
More you practise, the more confident become you.
The most you practise, the confident you become.
The more you practise, the more confident you become.
questions.e: Use “the + comparative, the + comparative” to show two linked changes.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I wish I had studied harder for the exam.
I wish I studied harder yesterday for the exam.
I wish I would have studied harder for the exam.
I wish I have studied harder for the exam.
questions.e: Use “wish + past perfect” to regret a past action.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Each of the players have received a medal.
Each of the players has received a medal.
Each players has received a medal.
Each of the player have received a medal.
questions.e: “Each” is singular, so use “has”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.e: “News” takes a singular verb in English.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: No sooner we had arrived than it started raining.
No sooner had we arrived when it started raining.
No sooner did we arrived than it started raining.
No sooner had we arrived than it started raining.
questions.e: Use inversion after “no sooner” and pair it with “than”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She would rather walk than wait for the bus.
She would rather to walk than wait for the bus.
She would rather walking than to wait for the bus.
She would rather walked than wait for the bus.
questions.e: Use the base verb after “would rather” and “than”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: By next June, she will works here for ten years.
By next June, she will have worked here for ten years.
By next June, she has worked here for ten years.
By next June, she will have work here for ten years.
questions.e: Use “will have + past participle” for a duration completed by a future time.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The teacher, along with her students, are attending the meeting.
The teacher along with her students attend the meeting yesterday.
The teacher, along with her students, is attending the meeting.
The teacher, with her students, were attending the meeting.
questions.e: The main subject is singular “teacher”; the phrase after it does not change the verb.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is believed that he left the country.
He is believed to left the country.
He believed to have left the country.
He is believed to have left the country.
questions.e: Use “is believed + to have + past participle” for a reported earlier action.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
Unless you will hurry, you miss the bus.
Unless you hurried, you will missed the bus.
Unless you don't hurry, you will miss the bus.
questions.e: “Unless” already means “if not”; use the present after it for a future possibility.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She speaks as though she knows the answer yesterday.
She speaks as though she knew the answer.
She speaks as though she would knew the answer.
She speaks as though she know the answer.
questions.e: Use a past form after “as though” to describe an unreal situation.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Having finish the assignment, he went outside.
Having finished the assignment, he has go outside.
Having finished the assignment, he went outside.
Having finishing the assignment, he went outside.
questions.e: Use “having + past participle” for an action completed before another past action.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The book who you lent me is fascinating.
The book which you lent me it is fascinating.
The book whom you lent me is fascinating.
The book that you lent me is fascinating.
questions.e: Use “that” or “which” for a thing, not “who” or “whom”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I would have helped if you had asked me.
I would help if you had asked me yesterday.
I would have helped if you would ask me.
I had helped if you have asked me.
questions.e: The past conditional uses “would have + past participle” with “if + had + past participle”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Little she knew that the road was closed.
Little did she know that the road was closed.
Little did she knew that the road was closed.
Little has she know that the road was closed.
questions.e: After “little” at the beginning, use inversion with “did + base verb”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Neither the coach nor the players was ready.
Neither the coach or the players were ready.
Neither the coach nor the players were ready.
Neither the coach nor the players is ready yesterday.
questions.e: With “neither…nor”, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, “players”.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: It is essential that every applicant is present.
It is essential every applicant to be present.
It is essential that every applicant was present.
It is essential that every applicant be present.
questions.e: After “It is essential that”, formal English can use the base form “be”.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly expresses an unreal past condition?
o: If I had known, I would have called you.
If I knew, I would have called you yesterday.
If I had known, I will call you.
If I would have known, I called you.
questions.e: Use past perfect in the if-clause and “would have” plus a participle in the result.

questions.q: Which sentence uses inversion after “hardly”?
o: Hardly we had arrived when the meeting began.
Hardly had we arrived when the meeting began.
Hardly did we arrived when the meeting began.
Hardly had we arrive than the meeting began.
questions.e: “Hardly” at the beginning requires auxiliary inversion.

questions.q: Which sentence has correct agreement with “neither…nor”?
o: Neither the teachers nor the principal are available.
Neither teachers or the principal is available.
Neither the teachers nor the principal is available.
Neither the principal nor the teachers is available yesterday.
questions.e: With “neither…nor,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses the passive voice?
o: The results published last week by the team.
The results was published last week.
The team were published the results last week.
The results were published last week.
questions.e: The passive uses “be” plus the past participle.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly reports a question?
o: He asked whether I had completed the report.
He asked whether had I completed the report.
He asked did I complete the report.
He asked whether I have complete the report.
questions.e: Reported questions use statement word order and backshift when appropriate.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly expresses regret about the past?
o: I wish I listened to your advice yesterday.
I wish I had listened to your advice.
I wish I would listen to your advice yesterday.
I wish I have listened to your advice.
questions.e: Use “wish” plus past perfect to regret a past action.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses “despite”?
o: Despite of the delay, the team finished the work.
Despite the team was delayed, they finished.
Despite the delay, the team finished the work.
Despite to the delay, the work was finished.
questions.e: “Despite” is followed by a noun phrase, not “of”.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly begins with “not only”?
o: Not only she proposed an idea, but she also defended it.
Not only did she proposed an idea, but she defended it.
Not only she did propose an idea, but also defended it.
Not only did she propose an idea, but she also defended it.
questions.e: An auxiliary comes before the subject after fronted “not only.”

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses “no sooner”?
o: No sooner had he left than the phone rang.
No sooner he had left than the phone rang.
No sooner had he left when the phone rang.
No sooner did he left than the phone rang.
questions.e: Use inversion and pair “no sooner” with “than.”

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive?
o: It is essential that every applicant is present.
It is essential that every applicant be present.
It is essential that every applicant was present tomorrow.
It is essential for every applicant being present.
questions.e: After “it is essential that,” formal English may use the base subjunctive “be.”

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses a relative pronoun for a person?
o: The teacher to which I spoke was helpful.
The teacher whom I spoke was helpful to.
The teacher to whom I spoke was helpful.
The teacher to who I spoke was helpful.
questions.e: Use “whom” as the object of the preposition “to” in formal English.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly expresses an unreal present condition?
o: If she would have more time, she learned another language.
If she has more time, she would learned another language.
If she had more time, she will learn another language.
If she had more time, she would learn another language.
questions.e: Use past simple in the if-clause and “would” plus base verb in the result.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly expresses a past unreal result?
o: If they had left earlier, they would have caught the train.
If they left earlier, they would have caught the train yesterday.
If they had left earlier, they would catch the train yesterday.
If they would have left earlier, they caught the train.
questions.e: The third conditional uses past perfect and “would have” plus a participle.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a participle clause correctly?
o: Having finish the report, Mariama sent it to her manager.
Having finished the report, Mariama sent it to her manager.
Finished the report, Mariama having sent it.
Having finished the report, it was sent by Mariama.
questions.e: The participle clause and main clause should have the same subject.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses a gerund after “avoid”?
o: They avoided to discuss the issue in public.
They avoided discuss the issue in public.
They avoided discussing the issue in public.
They avoided discussed the issue in public.
questions.e: “Avoid” is followed by a gerund.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses “unless”?
o: Unless you will hurry, you miss the bus.
Unless you hurried, you will miss the bus tomorrow.
Unless you don't hurry, you will miss the bus.
Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
questions.e: “Unless” means “if not”; use present simple for this future condition.

questions.q: Which sentence expresses a past possibility?
o: She might have taken the earlier train.
She might has taken the earlier train.
She might have take the earlier train.
She might took the earlier train.
questions.e: Use a modal plus “have” and a past participle for a past possibility.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses the future perfect?
o: By June, they will completed the project.
By June, they will have completed the project.
By June, they have completed the project tomorrow.
By June, they will have complete the project.
questions.e: The future perfect is “will have” plus a past participle.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses “would rather”?
o: I would rather you do not shared the document.
I would rather you not to share the document.
I would rather you did not share the document.
I would rather you had not share the document tomorrow.
questions.e: “Would rather” can be followed by a past form for a preference about another person.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses “so…that”?
o: The road was so narrow than two cars could not pass.
The road was such narrow that two cars could not pass.
The road was so narrow for two cars could not pass.
The road was so narrow that two cars could not pass.
questions.e: Use “so” plus an adjective and “that” before the result.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly compares countable nouns?
o: Fewer students chose the afternoon session this year.
Less students chose the afternoon session this year.
Fewer student chose the afternoon session this year.
Few students chose than the afternoon session this year.
questions.e: Use “fewer” with plural countable nouns.

questions.q: Which sentence uses “whom” as an object?
o: Who did the committee invite to spoke?
Whom did the committee invite to speak?
Whom invited the committee to speak?
Whom did the committee invited to speak?
questions.e: “Whom” is the object of “invite”; use the base verb after “did.”

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses “had it not been for”?
o: Had it not been for her help, we will miss the deadline.
Had it not been her help, we would missed the deadline.
Had it not been for her help, we would have missed the deadline.
If had it not been for her help, we missed the deadline.
questions.e: “Had it not been for” is an inverted form of a past conditional.

questions.q: Which sentence uses “not until” with correct inversion?
o: Not until the results arrived we made a decision.
Not until did the results arrive we make a decision.
Not until the results had arrived we did made a decision.
Not until the results arrived did we make a decision.
questions.e: When “not until” begins the sentence, invert the auxiliary and subject in the main clause.

questions.q: If I ___ more time, I would learn another language.
questions.e: Use the simple past in the “if” clause of this unreal situation.

questions.q: The report ___ by the committee last week.
questions.e: The past passive uses “was” plus a past participle.

questions.q: She said that she ___ the results the following day.
questions.e: In reported speech, “will” often changes to “would”.

questions.q: The students, ___ projects won prizes, thanked their teacher.
questions.e: Use “whose” to show that something belongs to people.

questions.q: By next June, he ___ at the school for ten years.
questions.e: Use the future perfect for an action completed by a future time.

questions.q: Neither the coach nor the players ___ satisfied.
questions.e: With “neither…nor”, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.q: The results ___ tomorrow morning.
questions.e: Use the future passive when the subject receives the action.

questions.q: She wishes she ___ closer to her family.
questions.e: Use the past form after “wish” for an unreal present situation.

questions.q: Hardly ___ the meeting begun when the power went out.
questions.e: Use inversion with “hardly” and the past perfect.

questions.q: The proposal was rejected, ___ surprised the team.
questions.e: Use “which” to refer to the whole previous idea.

questions.q: If they had left earlier, they ___ the traffic.
questions.e: Use “would have” plus a past participle for an unreal past result.

questions.q: The manager insisted that every form ___ signed.
questions.e: After “insist that”, formal English can use the base form.

questions.q: Not only ___ she finish early, but she also helped her classmates.
questions.e: Use “did” before the subject in this inversion.

questions.q: I would rather you ___ the issue in private.
questions.e: Use the past form after “would rather” for a preference.

questions.q: The claim ___ further evidence before publication.
questions.e: A general claim takes the simple present.

questions.q: Despite ___ warned, he continued the journey.
questions.e: After “despite”, use a noun or an -ing form.

questions.q: The harder she worked, ___ her results became.
questions.e: Use “the + comparative” in a paired comparison.

questions.q: The evidence is insufficient; ___, we cannot draw a conclusion.
questions.e: “Therefore” introduces a logical result.

questions.q: No sooner had they arrived ___ the rain started.
questions.e: The fixed expression is “no sooner…than”.

questions.q: He denied ___ the confidential document.
questions.e: After “deny”, use a verb ending in -ing.

questions.q: The policy aims to reduce waste, ___ costs in the long term.
questions.e: “Thereby” is followed by an -ing form.

questions.q: She speaks as though she ___ the entire project.
questions.e: Use the past perfect for an unreal earlier situation.

questions.q: The data, together with the appendix, ___ available online.
questions.e: The main subject “data” is treated here as a singular mass noun.

questions.q: Only after the review ___ the team understand the risk.
questions.e: Use inversion after the fronted phrase “only after”.

questions.q: The bridge ___ by local engineers last year.
questions.e: Au passif au passé, on utilise was + participe passé.

questions.q: “I am tired,” she said. She said that she ___ tired.
questions.e: Au discours rapporté au passé, am devient was.

questions.q: The new library ___ since the beginning of the year.
questions.e: Au present perfect passif, on dit has been + participe passé.

questions.q: The student ___ won the prize thanked her teacher.
questions.e: Who reprend une personne.

questions.q: By the time we arrived, the film ___.
questions.e: Had started marque l’action terminée avant une autre action passée.

questions.q: The report must ___ before Friday.
questions.e: Après must, le passif se forme avec be + participe passé.

questions.q: She asked me where I ___ the previous day.
questions.e: Dans le discours rapporté, l’action antérieure devient had gone.

questions.q: Unless you ___ now, you will miss the bus.
questions.e: Après unless, on utilise le présent pour parler d’une condition future.

questions.q: The book, ___ was written in Senegal, is available online.
questions.e: Which reprend un objet ou une chose.

questions.q: He wishes he ___ more carefully for the exam.
questions.e: Après wishes pour un regret présent, on emploie souvent le passé simple.

questions.q: Not only ___ the speech, but she also answered questions.
questions.e: Après Not only en tête, l’auxiliaire précède le sujet.

questions.q: The roads were flooded; ___, the school remained open.
questions.e: However marque une opposition.

questions.q: The teacher recommended that each student ___ a dictionary.
questions.e: Après recommend that, la forme de base bring est possible.

questions.q: The man ___ car was stolen reported it to the police.
questions.e: Whose indique la possession.

questions.q: By next June, they ___ the new classroom.
questions.e: Will have completed exprime une action achevée avant une date future.

questions.q: If she had left earlier, she ___ the train.
questions.e: Pour une condition passée irréelle, on dit would have + participe passé.

questions.q: The message ___ before the meeting began.
questions.e: Au passif au past perfect, on dit had been + participe passé.

questions.q: He denied ___ the confidential file.
questions.e: Après deny, le verbe prend souvent la forme en -ing.

questions.q: The results were so unclear that they ___ a second study.
questions.e: Carry out veut dire mener une étude.

questions.q: Despite ___ the instructions, he made the same error.
questions.e: Après despite, on peut utiliser un nom ou un verbe en -ing.

questions.q: The company reduced costs, ___ helped it remain competitive.
questions.e: Which peut reprendre toute l’idée de la proposition précédente.

questions.q: She would rather ___ at home than travel in the storm.
questions.e: Après would rather, on utilise la forme de base du verbe.

questions.q: The more you practise, the ___ you become.
questions.e: The more..., the more... sert à comparer deux évolutions.

questions.q: Only after the review ___ the error.
questions.e: Après Only after en tête, l’auxiliaire précède le sujet.
